newsitem.title: USA: FDA panel backs Rhone-Poulenc angina drug.
newsitem.headline: FDA panel backs Rhone-Poulenc angina drug.

text.p: A U.S. Food and Drug Administration advisory panel on Thursday voted 6-2 to approve a new use of Rhone-Poulenc Rorer's enoxaparin sodium (Lovenox).
The panel backed use of the drug for subcutaneous injection in patients experiencing unstable angina or non Q-wave heart attacks.

A majority of the panel said that Lovenox, a low molecular weight heparin, was superior to fractionated heparin, and that the one trial RPR submitted was positive. The FDA is not bound by its panels' advice but usually follows it.

Both conditions involve partial artery blockage and usually require emergency disillusion of clots. They result in 750,000 to one million hospitalizations a year in the United States. RPR submitted data from the Essence study, a 3,100-patient, 10-nation trial, hoping to convince the panel that it had proved its case with one trial.
In general, FDA has required two rigorous placebo-controlled trials. But in March 1997, the agency proposed in certain circumstances to allow just one.
RPR repeatedly referred to the document, saying that the Essence trial fell within the FDA guidelines.

Patients who came to the hospital with symptoms were assigned to two study arms: Lovenox plus a placebo injection and aspirin, or conventional heparin plus a placebo injection and aspirin. They were treated within 24 hours of the last angina attack, and given Lovenox for a minimum of 48 hours and up to eight days.
At two weeks, 19.8 percent of heparin patients had either died, had a heart attack, or recurrent chest pain, compared to 16.6 percent of the Lovenox patients.
A month later, 23.3 percent of heparin patients, and 19.8 percent of the Lovenox patients had had one of the events.

Marc Cohen, chairman of the ESSENCE study and a professor at Allegany University of the Health Sciences, said that Lovenox treatment was less expensive than heparin. Lovenox costs about $60 per day, depending on the patient's weight, and does not require intensive monitoring of blood levels as heparin does.
In the ESSENCE study, Lovenox patients had fewer days in the intensive care unit, and did not require as many by-pass or angioplasty procedures.

More Lovenox patients had minor bleeding episodes (18.4 percent compared to 14.2 percent), mostly due to injection site trauma. About 7 percent of patients in both groups had major bleeding episodes requiring transfusions or other measures, but there were no deaths during drug treatment.
Lovenox was first approved in the United States in 1993, and RPR sought approval for the new indication in March 1997.
The drug is also being evaluated in a study known as TIMI 11b, a 3,000-patient study to determine benefits and risks of long term treatment -- up to 45 days -- for unstable angina.
